questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reading for an argument
questions.learningObjective: Identify the argument a bundle summary is prepared to support
questions.stem: A clerk reads a bundle and notices that the summary of the hearing quotes only the parts of the transcript favouring one party.

options.text: Begin reading at the back of the bundle, where the conclusion and the counter-arguments are usually placed
options.misconception: assumes documents are ordered by argument structure

options.text: File a note that the transcript has been summarised unfairly, since a partial summary is a procedural irregularity
options.misconception: treats one-sided selection as a filing irregularity

options.text: Ask the other party to supply the missing extracts, since the bundle is the duty of the party that filed it
options.misconception: assumes the party who filed must correct the summary

options.text: Ask what argument the bundle supports, since a summary read for a purpose shapes what seems important

questions.explanation: A summary made for an argument will include what supports it and leave out what does not. The clerk's task is to identify the purpose of the summary before treating its silences as the absence of material.
questions.hint: Ask what the summary was written to show.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Turning a summary into a position
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a summary of events from a statement of position

stimulus.body: A file note summarises a hearing as follows: the application was opposed by two objectors, the council accepted the objections in part, and the matter was adjourned for further correspondence.

questions.stem: The clerk is asked to record the case's position in one line. Which line is defensible?

options.text: The application was opposed and therefore cannot succeed, since the council has shown where it stands
options.misconception: treats opposition as decisive on the outcome

options.text: The council has accepted part of the objections, but the application remains undecided pending correspondence
The application was granted in part, since the council has accepted some of the points raised against it
options.misconception: reads a partial acceptance of objections as a partial grant

options.text: The matter is closed with the objections upheld, since no further hearing date has yet been set
options.misconception: treats an adjournment as a final disposal

questions.explanation: A summary records what happened, while a position states what remains in dispute. The summary shows neither a refusal nor a grant, so the note must record the partial acceptance and the adjournment.
questions.hint: Ask what remains undecided in the note.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Questions that rule out an answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a question can foreclose the answer it seeks
questions.stem: A draft question asks whether the contractor could have completed the works by the contractual date. Explain why the question rules out the answer it is meant to find.

answer.exemplar: The question is framed around what could have been done, which assumes the works were late and makes failure the only possible answer. A question that can produce the opposite result would ask whether the works were completed by the contractual date and, if not, what caused the delay. As drafted, the contractor's answer is built in, so the inquiry never tests it, and the witness can only explain an assumption that has been handed to them.

questions.explanation: The word could presupposes failure, so a yes is the only available answer and the question cannot test the case it appears to open. Asking what happened, and if so why, would leave the outcome genuinely open.
questions.hint: Ask whether the opposite answer is possible.

questions.topic: Removing the assumption from a question
questions.learningObjective: Remove a presupposition from a question put to a witness
questions.stem: A clerk drafts a question for the witness: given that the survey was conducted to the required standard, how did the readings come to differ?

options.text: Keep the clause, since it protects the survey from suggestion and helps the witness answer carefully
options.misconception: values the appearance of fairness over the truth of the answer

options.text: Replace the question with one about who commissioned the survey, since the commissioner is the real issue
options.misconception: redirects the question away from the readings in issue

options.text: Drop the clause about the standard, then ask what the readings were and what procedure produced them
Keep the clause but reverse it, so the witness must show the survey was conducted to a poor standard
options.misconception: reverses the bias but keeps the question presupposing a conclusion

questions.explanation: A question that grants a fact asks the witness to build on it, and the answer then shows only how the granted fact leads on. Removing the assumption lets the readings and the procedure speak for themselves.
questions.hint: Ask what the question already takes to be true.

options.misconception: treats a large effect as proof of its cause

options.text: It credits the new timetable with the gain, so the note should add a longer history to strengthen the claim
options.misconception: supposes more supporting data repairs the causal gap

options.text: It credits the new timetable with the gain, so the note should drop the claim unless the operator can explain it
options.misconception: puts the burden of proof on the party that made the observation

options.text: It credits the new timetable with the gain, so the note should ask what else changed in the same weeks

questions.explanation: Timing is not attribution, and other changes in the same weeks could have produced the same gain. A note that credits one change must either rule out the rivals or say plainly that it cannot.
questions.hint: Ask what else could have changed at the same time.

options.misconception: keeps a scope that the available material cannot support

options.text: Research the depot's entire inspection history, since the wider record is needed before any conclusion is possible
options.misconception: widens the enquiry instead of narrowing it to the file

questions.topic: Answerability from available evidence
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a question is answerable from the material on file

stimulus.body: The bundle index lists a contract, a schedule of variations, two site photographs, and correspondence about payment. It does not list any record of the work having been carried out.

questions.stem: The clerk is asked whether the contractor carried out the work described in the contract. What does the file allow?

options.text: The question can be answered from the photographs, since a photograph of a site proves the work was completed
options.misconception: treats a site photograph as proof of completed work

options.text: The question cannot be answered from this bundle, since it holds nothing showing whether the work was done at all
The question can be answered from the correspondence, since a party disputing payment must have carried out the work
options.misconception: treats a party's position as an admission of the fact

options.text: The question can be answered once the contract is read, since the schedule of variations records the work as done
options.misconception: believes a contractual schedule records what was actually carried out

questions.explanation: Answerability follows the evidence: with no record of the work, the bundle supports what was agreed but not what was done. A clerk who answers anyway records an assumption as a finding.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reading for an argument
questions.learningObjective: State what a witness statement supports and what it leaves open
questions.stem: A clerk reads a witness statement and finds that it answers the question of damages but says nothing about the cause of the loss. Explain what the statement supports.

answer.exemplar: The statement is evidence on one question only, so it can be filed and read as an account of the loss and nothing more. The file must still establish the cause by other means, such as the correspondence, the inspection records or the testimony of the person who attended the site. A clerk who treats silence as agreement will close the file on a gap that nobody has filled, and that gap will be treated by the next reader as a point already covered by the witness's evidence.

questions.explanation: A statement answers the questions it takes up and is silent on the rest, and silence is not agreement. The cause of the loss must be established from other material in the file.
questions.hint: Ask which question the statement was taken to answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Turning a summary into a position
questions.learningObjective: Record a position that names what has been decided and what remains
questions.stem: A file note summarises an interlocutory hearing as: the court accepted the claimant's submissions on liability and made no order on the remedy.

options.text: The position is that the claim has been settled entirely, since liability was the only real issue in the action
options.misconception: treats one decided issue as disposing of the whole claim

options.text: The position is that the court rejected the claimant's case, since an order on remedy is always postponed
options.misconception: reads the deferral of remedy as a rejection

options.text: The position is that liability is settled in the claimant's favour while the remedy remains for a later hearing
The position is that the court is minded to dismiss the claim, since the claimant has been given time to prepare
options.misconception: reads a timetable adjustment as an indication of the outcome

questions.explanation: The two statements cover different issues, and the summary settles one while leaving the other open. Recording the position has to name both, so that no later reader treats the finding on liability as the end of the claim.
questions.hint: Ask which issues the summary has decided.

questions.topic: Questions that rule out an answer
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the presupposition built into a draft question
questions.stem: First, identify what the draft question assumes. Then choose the reply that removes the assumption.

options.text: It assumes the failure had already occurred, so the reply should ask whether failure occurred and what caused it
It assumes the failure had already occurred, so the reply should ask only what caused the failure to happen
options.misconception: accepts the presupposition and confines itself to the cause

options.text: It assumes nothing, since the question has been read by counsel and approved before being put to the witness
options.misconception: treats prior approval as proof that a question is neutral

options.text: It assumes the failure had already occurred, so the reply should ask the witness to accept that failure in terms
options.misconception: asks the witness to concede the very point in issue

questions.explanation: The question presupposes its own answer, which closes the field before the witness begins. Removing that presupposition means putting the failure itself in issue, and only then the cause.
questions.hint: Ask what answer the question allows the witness.

questions.topic: Removing the assumption from a question
questions.learningObjective: Take a disputed fact out of the wording of a question

options.text: Keep the delay clause, since the witness will confirm the delay and the question will then move to the date
options.misconception: assumes the disputed fact will be conceded by the witness

options.text: Keep the delay clause but remove the word could, so the witness must state positively whether the date was met
options.misconception: changes one modal verb while leaving the assumption in place

options.text: Replace the delay clause with a reference to the delivery records, since the records are a better foundation
options.misconception: swaps in a source that also presupposes the dispute

options.text: Remove the delay clause, since the delay is the very matter in dispute and should be put to the witness

questions.explanation: A question that grants a disputed fact makes the witness build on it, and the answer then shows only how the granted fact leads on. The assumption has to be taken out of the question itself.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Crediting a change for what followed it
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a causal claim against rival explanations for the same pattern

stimulus.body: A note records that noise complaints from the depot fell sharply in the six months after a new acoustic screen was installed, and concludes that the screen resolved the complaint.

questions.stem: Which criticism of the note is the strongest?

options.text: The note's conclusion is sound, because a fall in complaints over six months is more than chance could explain
options.misconception: treats a large effect as proof of its cause

options.text: The note credits the screen without asking whether complaints were also affected by a change in handling
The note should have set out the complaints for the same six months in each of the two preceding years
options.misconception: asks for a longer baseline while leaving the rival explanation untouched

options.text: The note should have recorded the individual complaints as well as the totals, since the totals hide the pattern
options.misconception: asks for more detail rather than addressing the attribution

questions.explanation: A fall in complaints can follow a change in how complaints are recorded or lodged, so the screen may not explain it. The note has to exclude such rival explanations before it credits the screen.
questions.hint: Ask what else could have reduced the number of complaints.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Narrowing a broad topic
questions.learningObjective: Reframe a research question so it matches the available material
questions.stem: A clerk is asked to research the lawfulness of the whole regulatory scheme. Explain how the enquiry should be reframed to fit the file and why.

answer.exemplar: A question about the lawfulness of the whole scheme asks for a judgment the file cannot support, because the documents on it touch only the enforcement of two particular powers and nothing about the scheme as a whole. The enquiry should be reframed to the validity of the exercise of those particular powers, which is the question the material can reach, while the file notes that the wider question remains outside the scope of this enquiry and should be raised separately by the party instructing.

questions.explanation: A research question has to match the material, and this file bears on particular decisions rather than the scheme in general. Narrowing it keeps the work answerable and marks the wider question as open.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions the documents actually touch.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Answerability from available evidence
questions.learningObjective: Separate what documents show from what they suggest about intention
questions.stem: A clerk is asked whether the parties intended the contract to be varied by email. Which assessment of the file is soundest?

options.text: The file can show what emails were sent and how they were answered, but not what the parties intended unless they said so
The file settles the question, because the parties' course of dealing in the emails shows their intention
options.misconception: treats conduct as conclusive proof of intention

options.text: The file settles the question, because the contract clause on variations governs the parties' intentions as well
options.misconception: assumes a clause about formalities determines subjective intention

options.text: The file cannot be touched at all, since a question about intention lies wholly outside a document review
options.misconception: overstates the limits of what the documents can show

questions.explanation: Documents record what was said and done, and intention is visible only where it was expressed. The file can support a finding about the emails and leave the question of intention open unless the parties addressed it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the parties said what they intended.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reading for an argument
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a bare denial in a pleading
questions.stem: A clerk reads the pleadings and finds that the reply denies the allegation but pleads no positive case. Explain what this tells the reader about the party's position.

answer.exemplar: A bare denial is a complete answer to the allegation and no more, so the pleadings leave the party's position defined only by what is alleged against it. The clerk should note that no positive case has been advanced, and should not infer from the silence that the allegation is admitted, because silence in a pleading is a position and not an acknowledgment. Any positive case would have to appear in the evidence at trial, and the file note should say which of the two is expected.

questions.explanation: Denial without positive case is a complete answer and no more, so the pleadings define the party's position by the allegation alone. Silence is a position to be noted, not an admission to be inferred.
questions.hint: Ask what silence in a pleading does and does not mean.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the reasons given by a court from the arguments recited

options.text: An accurate summary of the case, since a judgment that recites both sides fairly is the best account of it
options.misconception: treats a judgment's recital as the more reliable summary of the case

options.text: A decision with its reasons, since a reasoned conclusion lets a reader test it against the case advanced
A statement of the law, since reasons given by a court state the law that will apply in future cases
options.misconception: assumes the reasons of a judgment are always statements of general law

options.text: A record of what was argued, since reasons and submissions are different things and only submissions were argued
options.misconception: confuses the court's reasons with the parties' arguments

questions.explanation: Reciting submissions is not the same as giving reasons, and only the second lets a reader see how the decision follows from the case advanced. Reasons can be tested; recitals cannot.
questions.hint: Ask whether the conclusion is worked through.

options.misconception: objects to length rather than to the presupposition

options.text: The question should name the statute, since a witness cannot answer without knowing which period is meant
options.misconception: seeks more particulars when the real defect is the assumption

options.misconception: keeps the assumption while claiming the new wording puts it in issue

options.text: Replace the question with one about the cost of the survey, since cost is what the other side will attack
options.misconception: redirects the question to a different subject to avoid the difficulty

options.misconception: supposes more figures settle the question of attribution

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Turning a summary into a position
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a summary of what was said from the file's position
questions.stem: A file note summarises a witness's account and a counsel then asks what the file's position is on the disputed issue. Explain the difference between the two.

answer.exemplar: A summary is a record of what was said, arranged for reference, whereas a position is the conclusion the file as a whole supports on a particular issue, with the material behind it identified. The two come apart when a summary is written from one document rather than from the file as a whole, and they come apart again where a summary records a witness's opinion as though it were a finding. A clerk asked for the position must go back to the evidence and say what it shows, not what the note says.

questions.explanation: A summary records what was said; a position states what the file supports and identifies the material behind it. A clerk asked for the position must reason from the evidence rather than quote a note.
questions.hint: Ask what the file shows as against what a note records.

questions.explanation: The note separates what was ordered from what was heard, and only the costs order was decided. The position is a case standing adjourned, and recording more would report a disposal that has not happened.
questions.hint: Ask what was decided, as against what was only heard.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Questions that rule out an answer
questions.learningObjective: Split a question that presupposes the failure it is meant to prove
questions.stem: A clerk is asked to write a question that will establish the respondent's failure to notify. Explain why the question as usually drafted fails and how to write it.

answer.exemplar: The question usually asks why the respondent did not notify, which presupposes the failure and asks the witness to explain it. A witness who disputes the failure must then answer a question that has already assumed it, and any answer the witness gives is shaped by that assumption rather than by the evidence. The question should be split so that the witness is asked whether notification was given, in what form and on what date, and only then why the form used was said not to comply. That sequence allows the same witness to answer whether before being asked why.

questions.explanation: A question that presupposes the failure cannot be answered by a witness who disputes it, since the premise constrains the answer. The question must ask whether notification was given before asking why the form used was deficient.
questions.hint: Ask whether the failure is disputed before drafting around it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Removing the assumption from a question
questions.learningObjective: Identify the scope of an acceptance given by a witness

stimulus.body: A draft note reads: the witness accepted that the second inspection had taken place on 14 May, so she cannot now say the second inspection was never carried out.

questions.stem: What is the fault in the draft note?

options.text: It is faultless, since a witness who accepts a fact cannot afterwards deny that the fact occurred
options.misconception: treats acceptance as an irrevocable concession regardless of its terms

options.text: The fault is that the note refers to the second inspection, since the order of the inspections is not in issue
options.misconception: objects to an irrelevant detail while the misattribution goes unremarked

options.text: The fault is that the note asserts what the witness cannot say, which puts words in the witness's mouth
options.misconception: objects to the note's phrasing while missing the point about acceptance

options.text: It treats one acceptance as settling the point, when the acceptance may have been to a narrower proposition

questions.explanation: An acceptance is only as wide as the proposition put, and a witness who accepts that an inspection happened on a date has not accepted that it was a compliant one. The note must record what was accepted.
questions.hint: Ask what proposition the acceptance was given to.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Crediting a change for what followed it
questions.learningObjective: Test the direction of causation asserted in a file note
questions.stem: A clerk writes that the closure of the level crossing caused the rise in vehicle numbers at the junction. Which criticism is strongest?

options.text: The note should have cited the vehicle counts for the same quarter, so the reader can see the scale of the rise
options.misconception: asks for figures that would not reveal a reversed causal order

options.text: The note is sound, because the crossing closed first and the counts for the following quarter were higher
options.misconception: treats sequence alone as settling the direction of causation

options.text: The note should have quoted the residents, since their accounts of the junction are the best evidence of the cause
options.misconception: suggests anecdotes where the point is the direction of the causal claim

options.text: The note reverses the likely order, since a rise in vehicles would produce pressure for closure rather than follow it

questions.explanation: The note asserts a direction of causation that the file's own facts tell against, and no additional figure will repair that. Where cause and effect run the other way, the note must be rewritten rather than evidenced.
questions.hint: Ask which way round the causes would run.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Narrowing a broad topic
questions.learningObjective: Narrow a research request to the decisions that are on file
questions.stem: First, identify what the research request covers. Then choose the reply that brings it within reach.

options.text: It covers the fairness of the scheme as a whole, so the research should be accepted as the party framed it
options.misconception: treats a broad scope as legitimate because it came from the party

options.text: It covers the fairness of the scheme as a whole, so the clerk should decline the point as beyond the file's reach
options.misconception: declines the whole enquiry instead of narrowing it to the answerable part

options.text: It covers the fairness of the scheme as a whole, so the note should record the fairness question as answered in outline
options.misconception: records an outline of the general question as though it were researched

options.text: It covers the fairness of the scheme as a whole, so it should be narrowed to the two decisions on the file

questions.explanation: A request about fairness in general cannot be answered from the papers of two decisions, and a note that pretended otherwise would be asserting an opinion. Narrowing keeps the work answerable and marks the general question as open.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions the file actually contains.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Answerability from available evidence
questions.learningObjective: Choose how to read a bundle so that the arguments in it are visible
questions.stem: A clerk reads a bundle of documents produced in proceedings. Which approach to reading it is most useful?

options.text: Read it chronologically and in full, since completeness protects a clerk from missing anything in the pages
options.misconception: believes volume of reading is the same as understanding the case

options.text: Read it for the points on which the documents conflict, since that is where the case will actually be decided
Read only the documents that support the position the instructing party has already taken, since the rest are irrelevant
options.misconception: treats a party's existing case as a filter on what the file contains

options.text: Read the index and the summaries first, then the documents only if the summaries prove insufficient
options.misconception: treats a summary as a substitute for the source it summarises

questions.explanation: The useful reading of a bundle is the disagreement within it, since that is where the case is won or lost. Reading for completeness, for a party's case, or for the summaries instead of the sources all miss that.
questions.hint: Ask where the documents contradict each other.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reading for an argument
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what an email shows against what it leaves open

stimulus.body: A counsel note says the witness had no time to read the report before the meeting, and therefore the meeting could not have been a fair one. The file contains an email from the witness asking to bring the report forward to the meeting.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the file?

options.text: That the meeting was unfair, since the witness's own email proves the time was insufficient
options.misconception: treats a request to prepare as proof the preparation did not happen

options.text: That the meeting was fair, since the request shows the witness wanted to attend and had time to ask
options.misconception: treats the making of a request as proof that the request was granted

options.text: That the witness had sought to prepare for the meeting, since the email shows a request to bring the report forward
That the question of fairness cannot be reached, since no document records how long the meeting was
options.misconception: declares the question unanswerable when the documents show one relevant fact

questions.explanation: The email establishes that the witness asked to prepare, which the note omits and which bears on fairness. It does not settle the question, and the file should record it as evidence rather than as the answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the email shows and what it leaves open.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Turning a summary into a position
questions.learningObjective: Record what a conference settled and what it left undetermined
questions.stem: A clerk must record the outcome of a conference where the parties settled the amount of the claim but said nothing about costs. Explain what the note should say.

answer.exemplar: The conference settled the sum and nothing else, so a note that says the claim was settled would state more than happened. The note should record that the sum was agreed and the figure, and that costs were not mentioned and so remain to be determined, and it should identify who will confirm the agreement in writing, because a settlement of a sum is not complete until the parties have recorded it and the claim is not disposed of while costs are outstanding. A later reader of the file must be able to see exactly what was and was not concluded.

questions.explanation: A note that says the claim was settled states more than the conference settled, because costs were left open. The note should record the sum agreed, the silence on costs and what remains to be done.
questions.hint: Ask what was concluded and what was left out.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a question takes for granted and remove it
questions.stem: First, identify what the question takes for granted. Then choose the reply that removes the assumption.

options.text: It takes the defect in the barrier for granted, so the reply should ask whether the barrier was defective at all
It takes the defect in the barrier for granted, so the reply should ask only how long the defect had been present
options.misconception: accepts the presupposition and narrows the question to its duration

options.text: It takes nothing for granted, since the question has been settled with the other side and may not be put
options.misconception: treats an agreed form of words as proof that it is neutral

options.text: It takes the defect in the barrier for granted, so the reply should ask the witness to accept that the barrier was defective
options.misconception: asks the witness to concede the very point in issue

questions.explanation: A question that grants the defect lets the witness explain only what follows from it, and the defect is the matter in issue. The reply has to ask whether the barrier was defective before asking why it was not repaired.
questions.hint: Ask what the question lets the witness assume.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Removing the assumption from a question
questions.learningObjective: Repair a question that grants the disputed point about certification
questions.stem: A clerk drafts a question asking whether the crane was certified for that load, given that the certificate had expired. Explain the problem and the repair.

answer.exemplar: The question grants that the certificate had expired, which is the point the operator disputes, and it asks about the crane's fitness as though the load and the certification were settled. The repair is to split it: first what certificate the crane held and what it covered, then whether the load on the day was within it, and only then any consequence the witness says followed. Written in that order the operator can answer the certification question without having first accepted the expiry, and the witness is asked to speak to what the certificate says rather than to accept what is alleged.

questions.explanation: Granting the expiry puts the disputed fact into the question, and the answer then develops the assumption rather than the evidence. The question has to ask what the certificate covered before asking what followed from it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the expiry is agreed or disputed.
